div.p: The task schedulability theorem in the celebrated GRMS theory provides a sufficient condition only, specifying the upper bound on CPU utilization by scheduled periodic tasks. This paper presents a simulation study on real-time task scheduling for a specific case when the upper bound on processor utilization can be exceeded. The results are applied in a problem of multiprocessor task scheduling.
I.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Task scheduling in a real-time system has been a dynamically developing research field. Generalized Rate Monotonic Scheduling (GRMS) is a useful tool which enabling a system developer to achieve the real-time requirements [13,19]. GRMS assures that all tasks meet their deadlines as long as utilization of the system by all the tasks does not exceed some bound and appropriate algorithms for task scheduling are used. This theory has been successfully used in many serious research projects, for example space station programs and complex control systems [12,15].

In real-time control applications, a computer is hooked into a control plant in the (negative) feedback structure. It is well known that the control performance is very sensitive to delays occurring in the control loop. Now, if a delay in the control loop, which corresponds to an execution time for some computational task, exceeds a certain deadline, the whole process can go out of control. Applications in which violating by computer some prespecified task deadlines can result in any sort of a disaster are known as Hard Real-Time Systems [5]. On the other hand, there are also Soft Real-Time Systems which do not need hard limits, for example image transmission/recovery, where time limits do exist but they are not critical [7]. For instance, we can imagine an emergency situation in the image transmission system arising when the signal packet does not arrive in a strictly prespecified time limit. In result of such a fault we notice the stoppage of video transmission, but the failure does not evoke any disaster consequences [14,16,17,18,20].

Obviously, computing efficiency for real-time systems shall be modeled with much more caution than in the case of general-purpose computers. Collection of a sufficient amount of experimental data in order to verify if the system fulfills high reliability requirements would take too much time. Therefore, the task of modeling, simulation and evaluation of real-time systems is an important problem which is tackled in this paper by means of statistical tools.

div.head: II. BASIC CONCEPTS OF GRMS THEORY
div.p: A periodic task τ i is usually characterized by the worst case computation time C i and the period T i . It is usually assumed that the periodic task has to be finished before its own period is terminated. The tasks are considered independent if they do not require to synchronize with each other. A typical real-time system contains both periodic and aperiodic tasks. Using a simple polling procedure or a more advanced technique like sporadic-tasks server, the GRMS theory can be adopted to the case of aperiodic tasks as well [11].

According to the GRMS theorem, the set of N independent periodic tasks is always schedulable, i.e. all the tasks are executed within their deadlines (equal to the periods of task activation) if a GRMS algorithm for task scheduling (also called a rate monotonic algorithm) is used and the following inequality is fulfilled:
where: N -number of the tasks subject to the scheduling process C i -time of execution of the ith task T i -period of activation of the ith task.
A GRMS algorithm for task scheduling operates according to a few simple rules:
• Appropriate priorities are assigned to the tasks.

• Importance (height) of a specific priority is reversely proportional to the period of task activation -thus the tasks with shorter periods receive higher priorities. • At a given time instant, the task with the highest priority is always executed. • Activation of the task with higher priority causes an automatic and immediate expropriation of the task with lower priority. • The task that was expropriated could renew its execution only in case when there are no tasks with higher priority currently ready to be executed. The factor C i /T i is the utilization of the resource by the ith task. The right-hand side of inequality (1) provides the bound on the processor utilization (depending on the number N of scheduled tasks), below which a set of tasks is schedulable, i.e. deadlines will be met for all of these tasks. For high values of N, the right-hand side of inequality (1) quickly tends to the value ln2=0.6931. For example, the right-hand side of inequality (1) amounts to 0.6956 for N=100 and to 0.6934 for N=1000. Hence, in case of high-size independent periodic tasks, if the total utilization of the processor does not exceed 69.31% of time of its operation, then the set of periodic tasks is schedulable.

It is worth emphasizing that inequality (1) provides only a sufficient condition for schedulability of a given set of independent periodic tasks. That means that, in some cases, a set of independent periodic tasks may be schedulable even though inequality (1) is not satisfied.

Obviously, the necessary condition is that the total percentage of processor utilization by all the tasks would not exceed 100% since otherwise the fulfillment of deadlines for some tasks would not be possible.
The above considerations can be illustrated on a simple example. Consider two periodic tasks:

• Task No. 1 with the period T 1 =2ms and the execution time C 1 =1ms. • Task No. 2 with the period T 2 =4ms and the execution time C 2 =2ms. Notice that the total utilization of the processor operation time by the two tasks is just 100%. However, the considered set of tasks is schedulable, which can be easily verified from the time chart of Fig. 1. This paper presents an attempt at seeking for a "sort of" a cumulative distribution function of such an event that an arbitrarily given set of independent periodic tasks occupying the processor by more than 69% of time is schedulable. Precisely, we seek for a sort of a "reversive" cumulative distribution function F(s) for a random variable S being a percentage of processor occupation by the set of tasks under scheduling. The problem of finding an analytical form of the function F(s) has not been succeeded yet. Therefore, in order to analyze possible forms of the function it is resolved to perform a high number of computer simulations for the task scheduling problem and to statistically estimate the function F(s) for selected realizations s of the random variable S.

Since the GRMS theorem concerns a sufficient, rather than necessary condition for the task schedulability, the question arises what percentage of the GRMS-scheduled task plans are schedulable. A number of performed computer simulations enabled to answer that question.

Real-time systems are a very important and well-defined class of the computer systems. In a crude simplification, a real-time system is defined as a computer system in which computing results depend not only on data generated by the environment but they are also subordinated to the elapsing time. Now, a system delivering even logically correct results but violating the deadlines may cause a disaster to the environment [1,2,3,4,6,8,11].

Programs used in real-time computer systems are composed mostly of many tasks implementing given system's goals. Usually, each of these tasks supports only one of subunits of the plant under control. These tasks are usually implemented as periodic tasks, that is they are activated periodically. Also, they are mostly independent, i.e. they need no synchronization. Moreover, implementation of such tasks is subject to time deadlines, which are mostly equal to the period of their activation.

div.head: III. COMPUTER SIMULATION RESULTS
div.p: Numerous computer simulations were performed in order to evaluate the function F(s) in given points (tabularization of the function). Namely, for each value of the percentage of the processor utilization s, being a figure from the range 70% to 100%, a pseudo-random number generator (the rand() function in the C language) was used to generate one thousand various sets of independent periodic tasks totally utilizing the processor for the time percentage s. Then, using a stop test, each of the generated task sets was individually verified with respect of its schedulability.

The randomly generated tasks had their periods within the range of 10 to 1000 time units, whereas their execution times were in the range of 1 to 100 time units. Another (reasonable) constraint was that the execution time for each task could not exceed 10% of its period. Thus, none of the tasks could utilize the processor for more than 10% of time. Thus, the numbers of the scheduled tasks were rather low (a few or several tasks).

As a result of the performed simulations, numbers of schedulable task sets were obtained, with deadlines for all the tasks being met. Based on the obtained simulation results, a graph of a "sort of" a (reversive) cumulative probability distribution function is plotted in Fig. 2. Note that, for the physical interpretation reasons, the function is scaled in a number of scheduled task plans vs. processor load. As can be seen from Fig. 2, if the CPU load is less than 77%, a number of task scheduling plans is over 800 and if the CPU load is above 77%, a number of task scheduling plans is decreased dramatically. It can be concluded that the value of 77% is the limit load below which the processor task plans are schedulable.

div.head: IV. TASK SCHEDULING IN MULTIPROCESSOR SYSTEMS
div.p: The above simulation results can also be of interest in case of multiprocessor systems performing computation of very large sets of independent periodic tasks. In such a case, the percentage of utilizing a single processor could achieve very high values, largely exceeding the limit value of 100%. It is thus evident that such task sets cannot be subject to scheduling on a single processor and using a multiprocessor system is necessary to do the task scheduling job. However, the scheduling simulation results obtained for a single processor can provide means enabling to answer the important question: for a specific time percentage s of utilization of a single processor, with s>100%, how many processors must be used to meet the deadlines for all the tasks?

For example, if a certain, arbitrarily given set of tasks utilizes a single processor in 700%, then the set should be divided into 11 smaller subsets, each of which will use its own processor in no more than 69%. So, the deadlines for all the tasks will be met, but at the cost of employing as many as 11 computing units.

Well, but what if the number of used processors is reduced in that case to 10? Then, the average utilization of each computing unit will be 70%. So, given the inequality (1), it cannot be said that, after the above mentioned division into the task subsets, all of the tasks will be schedulable. However, one can estimate the probability of an event that the scheduling condition will be fulfilled. It can be easily found that this probability is (0.998) 10 =0.980, so that there is a quite good chance that such a division will be successful. Otherwise, one can attempt at some alternative division(s) into the task subsets allocated to the specified processors (a number of possible solutions is really huge leading to a combinatorial explosion).

In case of using just 9 processors, each of them would be loaded at an average of 77.8%, so that the probability of randomly obtaining 9 scheduled task subsets is (0.778) 9 = 0.104. This is not too much indeed, but at an average of 10 different, arbitrarily performed divisions of the original task set the deadlines should be met for all the tasks. Therefore, it is desirable to seek for such a successful division and the profit would be the two computing units saved.

Summing up, it can be said that the results shown in this chapter can be a basis for the assessment of a number of computing units utilized in real-time scheduling of a given task set. However, a precise solution to the multiprocessor task scheduling problem requires a detailed tabularization of a reversive probability distribution function.

div.head: V. TABULARIZATION OF REVERSIVE PROBABILITY DISTRIBUTION FUNCTION
div.p: Tabularization of a reversive cumulative probability distribution function F(s) is done with the 0.1% precision step of the processor load s, which is a tenfold densification as compared with the results of Fig. 2. This will enable to more precisely estimate the probability of forming schedulable task plans executed in parallel in a multiprocessor system.

Periods of randomly generated tasks ranged from 1000 to 100,000 time units, whereas their execution times varied from 1 to 100 time units. An additional constraint was that, for each task, its execution time could not exceed 0.1% of its period, that is none of the tasks used the processor time for longer than 0.1%. The intension was to have a very high number of scheduled tasks so that the right-hand side of inequality (1) could be close to 0.6931. Also, with the high number of tasks, each of which using the processor for a short time only, it is possible for the processor load factor s to quite precisely approach a prespecified value.

Clearly, the conditions for the realization of task scheduling simulations are now quite different from those earlier ones, because of the huge number of tasks attempted now at the scheduling process and each of these tasks using the processor for a short time only. Moreover, there were 10,000 tasks randomly generated for each load factor s and then they were subject to the GRMS scheduling process. This contributes to a high accuracy of estimation of the reverse probability distribution function. Results of the scheduling computer simulations are shown in Fig. 3 and these are, unsurprisingly, quite different from those of Fig. 2. Probability of schedulability of the task sets using the processor for time percentages 69.0% to 69.3% is equal to unity according to the GRMS theorem described by inequality (1). Similarly, the probability is "practically" equal to unity for the task sets using the processor for 69.4% to 75.5% time, although a case may occur that some set of tasks appears nonschedulable. Rather surprisingly, the probability is still higher than 0.9 for the processor loads ranging from 75.6% to 77.9% time. It is not before the load reaches the value of some 80.0% that the probability is rapidly decreased. Finally, the probability is practically zero for the loads exceeding some 83.5%, although a case may still occur that some task set appears schedulable.

div.head: VI. TASK ALLOCATION SCHEME IN A MULTIPROCESSOR
SYSTEM
div.p: A starting point for task allocation in a multiprocessor system is the determination of a total occupation of a computing unit by all the tasks subject to scheduling. Let the obtained total load equals for instance to 731%. The following procedure is recommended to calculate a number of processors to solve the task scheduling problem. Round the load figure up to the nearest multiplicity of 100, that is 800 in our example. Divide the obtained value by 100 to obtain a minimum number of computing units needed for the realization of the task scheduling problem, that is 8 in our example. Under an assumption on a high number of tasks, each of which using the processor for a short time only, one can use the scheduling results illustrated in Fig. 3. In our example, having uniformly distributed the tasks into all the computing units, an average load of each processor will be 731/8, that is 91.4%. Unfortunately, probability of scheduling an arbitrary task plan for such a load is practically zero. Therefore, increase a number of processors to 9 and repeat the calculations. Now, the average load is 731/9, that is 81.2% and the probability of task set schedulability is 0.062. That means that the probability of an event of schedulability of all the task plans is (0.062) 9 which is practically zero. So, increase a number of processors to 10. The average load is now 731/10, that is 71.3%, thus providing the schedulability probability for each task set being close to unity. Now, 10 processors are needed for the realization of the specific task scheduling problem, well, under the aforementioned assumption.

It is worth mentioning that novel multiprocessor task scheduling solutions employ intelligent optimization techniques, e.g. genetic algorithms [21,22]. Those solutions are more general, of course, but they are computationally involving as compared to our simple approach, which is valid, however, for specific multiprocessor systems only.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: The task schedulability theorem in the celebrated GRMS theory presents a sufficient condition for an upper bound for the total utilization of a computer resource by all the scheduled, independent periodic tasks. The bound is pessimistic, that is specific task set(s) can be schedulable even if the theorem's condition is not satisfied. To verify if task(s) scheduled on the resource with total utilization greater than the aforementioned bound can meet their deadlines one can use the exact schedulability test. To this end, computer simulations of such tests have been performed, making use of randomly generated task sets utilizing the resource for various time percentages. A sort of a (reversive) cumulative probability distribution function has been obtained, determining time percentages for schedulable task plans even in cases the theorem's bound condition is not fulfilled. The function constitutes a contribution to the GRMS theory for a class of periodic tasks under tests.
